questions.text: Boosting
questions.explanation: Boosting trains models sequentially, with each new model giving more weight to the observations the previous one got wrong. It's the ensemble family that primarily reduces bias by combining many weak learners into a strong one.

options.text: An ensemble technique that trains models sequentially, with each new model focusing more on the observations the previous model got wrong.
An ensemble technique that trains models in parallel on different bootstrapped samples and combines their outputs by voting or averaging.
An ensemble technique that trains a meta-model to learn how to best combine the predictions of several independently trained base models.
An ensemble technique that combines predictions from several independently trained models by majority vote or averaging, using a fixed rule.

questions.text: A team trains models one after another, and each new model gives extra weight to the observations the previous model got wrong, gradually turning weak learners into a strong one. Which ensemble technique are they using?
questions.explanation: Boosting trains models sequentially, with each new learner correcting the errors of the one before it by penalizing misclassified observations — this mainly reduces bias, unlike bagging's parallel, variance-reducing approach.

options.text: Boosting (sequential)
Bagging (bootstrap)
Voting ensemble
Stacking (meta-model)

questions.text: Bootstrapping aggregation
questions.explanation: Bagging trains multiple models in parallel, each on a different bootstrapped sample of the data, then combines their predictions by voting or averaging. It primarily reduces variance, which is why Random Forest applies it to decision trees.

options.text: An ensemble technique that trains models in parallel on different bootstrapped samples and combines their outputs by voting or averaging.
An ensemble technique that trains models sequentially, with each new model focusing more on the observations the previous model got wrong.
An ensemble technique that trains a meta-model to learn how to best combine the predictions of several independently trained base models.
A broad family of techniques that combine multiple models' predictions to produce a single, stronger prediction.

questions.text: A single decision tree is badly overfitting, so the team wants to train many trees in parallel on different bootstrapped samples and combine their predictions to cut variance. Which technique fits?
questions.explanation: Bootstrap aggregation (bagging) trains models independently and in parallel on bootstrapped samples, then averages or votes on their predictions, primarily to reduce variance — the standard fix for an overfitting decision tree.

options.text: Bagging (bootstrap)
Boosting (sequential)
Stacking (meta-model)
Voting ensemble

questions.text: Ensemble
questions.explanation: An ensemble combines multiple models' predictions, via voting or averaging, to produce a stronger prediction than any single model alone. Bagging, boosting, and stacking are the main families tested on the exam.

options.text: A broad family of techniques that combine multiple models' predictions, typically by voting or averaging, to produce one stronger prediction.
An ensemble technique that trains models in parallel on different bootstrapped samples and combines their outputs by voting or averaging.
An ensemble technique that trains models sequentially, with each new model focusing more on the observations the previous model got wrong.
An ensemble technique that trains a meta-model to learn how to best combine the predictions of several independently trained base models.

questions.text: A team wants to combine several models' predictions, using majority voting for classification or averaging for regression, so the final output generalizes better than any single model alone. What general approach are they using?
questions.explanation: Ensemble methods combine multiple models and aggregate their outputs via voting or averaging, generally improving generalization over relying on a single model.

options.text: Ensemble learning
Cross-validation
Hyperparameter tuning
Feature engineering

questions.text: Stacking
questions.explanation: Stacking trains several diverse base models and then a second-level meta-model that learns how to best combine their predictions. Unlike bagging or boosting, the combination rule is learned rather than fixed.

options.text: An ensemble technique that trains a meta-model to learn how to best combine the predictions of several independently trained base models.
An ensemble technique that trains models sequentially, with each new model focusing more on the observations the previous model got wrong.
An ensemble technique that trains models in parallel on different bootstrapped samples and combines their outputs by voting or averaging.
An ensemble technique that combines predictions from several independently trained models by majority vote or averaging, using a fixed rule.

questions.text: A competition team trains XGBoost, Random Forest, and a neural network independently, then fits a logistic regression model on their outputs to produce the final prediction. Which ensemble technique are they using?
questions.explanation: Stacking trains diverse base models independently and then trains a second-level meta-model to learn how to best combine their predictions, unlike voting's fixed combination rule.

options.text: Stacking (meta-model)
Voting ensemble
Boosting (sequential)
Bagging (bootstrap)

questions.text: Voting ensemble
questions.explanation: A voting ensemble combines predictions from independently trained, typically different models using a fixed rule — majority vote for classification or averaging for regression. It's simpler than stacking, which learns the combination instead.

options.text: An ensemble technique that combines predictions from several independently trained models by majority vote or averaging, using a fixed rule.
An ensemble technique that trains a meta-model to learn how to best combine the predictions of several independently trained base models.
An ensemble technique that trains models in parallel on different bootstrapped samples and combines their outputs by voting or averaging.
An ensemble technique that trains models sequentially, with each new model focusing more on the observations the previous model got wrong.

questions.text: A team combines predictions from a logistic regression model, a decision tree, and an SVM trained on the same data by taking a majority vote, with no model learning how to weight the others. Which technique is this?
questions.explanation: A voting ensemble combines predictions from independently trained, typically different models using a fixed rule (majority vote or average), unlike stacking, which learns the combination via a meta-model.

options.text: The voting ensemble
Stacking (meta-model)
Boosting (sequential)
Bagging (bootstrap)

questions.text: Bias drift
questions.explanation: Bias drift is a shift in a deployed model's fairness metrics over time relative to a training-time baseline, detected in AWS with SageMaker Model Monitor's bias drift monitoring. It's distinct from model drift, which tracks overall predictive performance rather than fairness.

options.text: A shift in a deployed model's fairness metrics over time relative to a baseline, causing it to treat groups differently than at training time.
A gradual decline in a deployed model's overall predictive performance caused by changes in input data or the input-target relationship.
A pre-training metric that measures whether a group experiences a disproportionate share of a negative outcome, conditioned on another attribute.
Error caused by a model's simplifying assumptions being too strong, leading it to underfit both training and validation data.

questions.text: Months after launch, a credit-approval model's overall accuracy is unchanged, but it now approves one demographic group at a disproportionate rate compared to when it was validated as fair. What should the team be monitoring to catch this?
questions.explanation: Bias drift is a shift in a deployed model's fairness metrics relative to a baseline over time, distinct from model drift, which concerns overall predictive performance decaying.

options.text: Bias drift
Model drift
High variance
High bias

questions.text: Bias errors
questions.explanation: Bias errors come from a model's simplifying assumptions being too strong to capture the true relationship in the data, causing underfitting on both training and validation sets. Linear models tend to have high bias; decision trees have less.

options.text: Error caused by a model's simplifying assumptions being too strong, leading it to underfit both training and test data.
Error caused by a model being overly sensitive to the specific training data, leading it to overfit and generalize poorly to new data.
A shift in a deployed model's fairness metrics over time relative to a baseline established during training.
A gradual decline in a deployed model's overall predictive performance after deployment, caused by changing input data.

questions.text: A linear regression model performs poorly on the training data itself, with both training and validation error high and roughly equal. What problem does this pattern indicate?
questions.explanation: High bias causes underfitting, where an overly simple model performs poorly on both training and validation data; the fix is a more flexible algorithm or added features, not more data.

options.text: High bias (underfitting)
High variance (overfitting)
Model drift (accuracy decay)
Bias drift (fairness shift)

questions.text: Conditional Demographic Disparity (CDD)
questions.explanation: Conditional Demographic Disparity is a pre-training bias metric computed by SageMaker Clarify that measures whether a group experiences a disproportionate share of a negative outcome, conditioned on another attribute to control for confounding variables.
questions.source: key-concepts/Error, Bias & Drift/🔑 Conditional Demographic Disparity (CDD).md

options.text: A pre-training bias metric that measures whether a group faces a disproportionate negative outcome, conditioned on another attribute.

A gradual decline in a deployed model's overall predictive performance after deployment, caused by changing input data.

questions.explanation: Conditional Demographic Disparity conditions the comparison on a confounding attribute (e.g., job category), avoiding the misleading conclusions a raw, unconditioned disparity comparison could produce.

options.text: A gradual decline in a deployed model's overall predictive performance over time, caused by changes in input data or the input-target relationship.
A shift in a deployed model's fairness metrics over time relative to a baseline, causing it to treat groups differently than at training time.
A pre-training metric that measures whether a group experiences a disproportionate share of a negative outcome, conditioned on another attribute.
Error caused by a model's simplifying assumptions being too strong, leading it to underfit both training and validation data.

questions.explanation: Model drift is the gradual degradation of a deployed model's predictive performance caused by shifts in input data or the input-target relationship, detected in AWS with SageMaker Model Monitor.

options.text: Model drift
Bias drift
High variance
High bias

questions.text: Variance errors
questions.explanation: Variance errors come from a model being overly sensitive to the specific training data, causing it to overfit and generalize poorly. Decision trees are a classic high-variance algorithm; bagging is a standard fix.

options.text: Error caused by a model being overly sensitive to the specific training data, leading it to overfit and generalize poorly to new data.
Error caused by a model's simplifying assumptions being too strong to capture the true relationship, leading it to underfit both training and test data.
A shift in a deployed model's fairness metrics over time relative to a baseline established during training.
A gradual decline in a deployed model's overall predictive performance after deployment, caused by changing input data.

questions.explanation: High variance causes overfitting, where a model fits training data very well but fails to generalize; fixes include pruning, regularization, more data, or bagging.

options.text: High variance (overfitting)
High bias (underfitting)
Model drift (accuracy decay)

questions.text: Accuracy
questions.explanation: Accuracy is the proportion of all predictions (both true positives and true negatives) that were correct. It's misleading on imbalanced datasets, where a model that always predicts the majority class can score high while being useless.

options.text: The proportion of all predictions that were correct, combining true positives and true negatives.
The proportion of predictions labeled positive by the model that were actually positive cases.
The proportion of actual positive cases that were correctly identified as positive by the model.
The harmonic mean of precision and recall, combining both into a single balanced metric.

questions.text: A fraud dataset is 99% legitimate transactions and 1% fraud, and a model that always predicts 'not fraud' scores very well on one common metric despite being useless. Which metric is misleading here?
questions.explanation: Accuracy is misleading on imbalanced datasets, since always predicting the majority class yields a high score without any real predictive value; precision, recall, or F1 are better fits.

options.text: Accuracy
F1 score
Recall
Precision

questions.text: AUC (Area Under the Curve)
questions.explanation: AUC condenses a performance curve, most commonly the ROC curve, into a single scalar between 0 and 1 that summarizes classifier performance across every threshold. An AUC of 0.5 means no better than random guessing.

options.text: A single number between 0 and 1 representing the area under a performance curve across thresholds.

The proportion of predictions labeled positive by the model that were actually positive cases.
The proportion of actual positive cases that were correctly identified as positive by the model.

questions.text: During a SageMaker tuning job, a team wants a single threshold-independent score to rank several candidate binary classifiers before committing to any operating threshold. Which metric should they use?
questions.explanation: AUC condenses classifier performance across every possible threshold into one scalar between 0 and 1, making it threshold-independent and well suited for comparing models before picking an operating point.

options.text: The area under the curve that plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate across classification thresholds.

questions.text: F1 score
questions.explanation: The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, giving one balanced number instead of two. It's the go-to metric for imbalanced datasets when there's no strong reason to favor precision or recall individually.

options.text: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, combining both into a single balanced metric at one chosen threshold.
The proportion of all predictions that were correct, combining true positives and true negatives, out of every prediction made.
The proportion of predictions labeled positive by the model that were actually positive cases.
The proportion of actual positive cases that were correctly identified as positive by the model.

questions.explanation: The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, giving a single balanced metric for imbalanced datasets when neither error type is clearly more costly.

options.text: F1 score
Accuracy
RMSE value

questions.text: Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
questions.explanation: MAE is the average of the absolute differences between predicted and actual values, expressed in the same unit as the target. It treats every error equally, making it more robust to outliers than RMSE.

options.text: A regression metric equal to the average of the absolute differences between predicted and actual values, treating every error equally.

questions.text: Precision
questions.explanation: Precision is the proportion of predictions labeled positive that were actually positive. It matters most when false positives are costly, such as a spam filter flagging legitimate email.

options.text: The proportion of predictions labeled positive by the model that were actually positive cases.
